proposals.impact: lift 37.5% open rate toward Money Vigilance baseline
proposals.observation: The Money Worship automation sent 16 emails and achieved a 37.5% open rate — nine percentage points below the Money Vigilance sequence (66.67%) and fifteen points below Money Avoidance (52.63%). Open rate differences at this scale are almost always subject-line driven, not content driven. The Money Worship sequence's email-1 subject line is the single cheapest fix available because it requires one line changed in one file.
proposals.proposal: Rewrite the subject line of Money Worship email 1. The current line is almost certainly making a promise that feels aspirational rather than recognised — something the reader sees as "that's for other people". Money Worship subscribers have told the quiz they tie self-worth to net worth. A subject that names the specific, slightly embarrassing behaviour (checking your savings balance for a mood boost, refreshing your investment app after a good day at work) will outperform a subject that describes an outcome. Replace the existing subject line with one that reflects a behaviour Joel's ICP actually does, drawn from the £150k story context: earning well, checking the number, feeling briefly okay, then spending to celebrate.

proposals.proposal: Draft and commit one new blog post targeting the Money Worship reader. The post should sit at the awareness end of the funnel: a reader who earns well, checks their portfolio more than once a day, and quietly uses their balance as a mood regulator. The title below reflects a real, specific, slightly uncomfortable behaviour rather than a category label. This is one new file added to src/content/blog/. No existing files are modified.
proposals.new_text:
---
title: "Why do I feel worse about money the more I earn?"
pubDate: "2026-07-29"
description: "You expected earning more to settle something. It did not. Here is what is actually going on when the number keeps moving and the feeling never quite follows."
tags: ["money worship", "self-worth", "behavioural money"]
draft: false
---

You got the pay rise. You hit the savings target you set two years ago. You refreshed the app and the number was higher than it had ever been.

You felt okay for about four hours.

Then something small went wrong — a slow afternoon, a friend mentioning their property, a Sunday with nothing to show for it — and the number stopped mattering.

This is not a discipline problem. It is not ingratitude. It is a pattern that Joel sees consistently in clients who earn well: the figure on the screen has been doing a job it was never built to do. It is being asked to confirm that you are enough. It cannot confirm that, no matter how many digits it gains.

Joel works with people in their late twenties and early thirties who are, by most measures, doing well. MSc Behavioural Economics | Qualified Financial Planner. The work is not budgeting. The work is understanding what the money is actually being asked to carry.

If the number going up does not produce the settled feeling you expected, that gap is worth looking at honestly.
